Keep polling/wait loops bounded, do not duplicate active work, and use stable `clientRequestId` values when retrying tools that accept them.

ACP fallback: some ACP agents accept the injected MCP server but fail to expose its tools. When the T3 tools are absent and `T3_ACP_MCP_NODE` is present, call the same tools through the terminal: `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 "$T3_ACP_MCP_NODE" ${T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT:+"$T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT"} acp-mcp-call orchestrator_capabilities '{}'` (`T3_ACP_MCP_ENTRYPOINT` is unset when T3 runs as a standalone executable). Delegate with `acp-mcp-call delegate_task '{"task":"...","target":{"providerInstanceId":"...","model":"..."},"mode":"async","clientRequestId":"..."}'`. This is the supported T3 transport fallback, not an ordinary shell-based substitute for delegation.

### Showing visuals

When a chart, table, diagram, image collage, or mockup would say more than prose, build a self-contained HTML page, check it with `html_preview`, then publish it with `html_render` before your final reply. The reader sees the page above that reply, so don't announce or restate it; add only what it doesn't say.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

Reach for this when the task matches an available agent type, when you have independent work to run in parallel, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate it and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps. For a single-fact lookup where you already know the file, symbol, or value, search directly. Once you've delegated a search, don't also run it yourself — wait for the result.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

channel.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

q.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: ShareOnboardingGuide
tools.description:
Upload the ONBOARDING.md in the current directory and return a share link teammates can open in Claude Code. Call this after the user has confirmed the final content.

When called with the default mode='check': if a local ONBOARDING.md is present, uploads it to the most-recently-updated org guide (or creates one if none exist) and returns a fresh link. If no local file is present, returns the existing link without uploading (status: has_existing).

mode.description: 'check' (default): if ONBOARDING.md is present locally, uploads it to the most-recent guide (creates one if none exist); otherwise reports the existing link without uploading. 'update': upload to a specific guide by short_code. 'create': always make a new link. 'delete': remove a guide.

short_code.description: Short code of a specific guide to target (returned by a previous call). Honored by check, update, and delete — skips the org-wide lookup and targets this guide directly.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

content.text:
I've pushed the fix to #1745 (`69244f4f`), updated the PR body, and linked the PR to this thread. The Matter suites pass (321 passed, 1 expected failure), and so do `test_base`, `test_event`, `test_architecture` and `prek`.

**What changed:** when a LockOperation event's `operationSource` is Keypad (3), the use is reported as `pin`, whatever `credentialType` says. This applies only to credentials the PR already reports, so two things are still dropped:
- the lock's admin code (type 0) used at the keypad;
- owine's Home Key events, because type 10 isn't a valid credential type.

**Two places I went narrower than option 1 as I described it:**
- **Keypad only.** I first added a card reader (`operationSource` 8) → `rfid` too. But no device has shown it's needed, and no test would notice if it were removed, so I took it out. Biometric (9) is left alone for the same reason; its `credentialType` still decides.
- **The PIN-index lookup still applies to these events.** A keypad event the lock logged as type 3 now counts as a PIN. When an event has no `userIndex`, LCM finds the user by walking for a PIN at `credentialIndex`. That would be wrong if this firmware also got the index wrong. owine's events all carried a correct `userIndex`, so the lookup never runs for them, and I kept the code simple rather than add a second flag.

**Tests:**
- An e2e test on the fake Matter lock: a keypad unlock logged with type 3 is recorded as `pin` for the right user.
- A unit test using owine's two captured events: the keypad PIN gives `pin`, the Home Key gives nothing.
- Removing the override makes both keypad tests fail.

**Draft reply to owine.** I haven't posted it:

> Thanks for the captures — they made this easy to pin down. In every event you posted, `credentialType` equals `operationSource` (3 = Keypad, 10 = Aliro), so the firmware looks to be writing the source into the type field.
>
> I've pushed 69244f4 to this PR: a Keypad-source use is now reported as `pin` regardless of `credentialType`, and your two payloads are in the tests verbatim. Home Key unlocks stay unreported. That isn't a lock problem: LCM doesn't report Aliro credentials from any lock yet.
>
> On 7.0.0 your keypad unlocks are dropped entirely, so with this build you should start seeing them on the user's event entity, labelled `pin`. If you can install the `fix/credential-type-of-use` branch and do a keypad unlock as `lcm:4:Gue`, confirming the event fires as `pin` would be great.

## owine @ 2026-10-18T19:01:16Z https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/pull/1745#issuecomment-6253867587
I have an Aqara U400 (Matter over Thread, firmware 3.1.1.0) that trips over this, so here's what it sends. Setup is HA 2026.10, LCM 7.0.0, and the Matter Server app 9.2.0 (matter-server 1.4.0 / matter.js 0.17.9).

The lock writes the operation source into `credentials[].credentialType` in its LockOperation events. A keypad PIN arrives as type 3, and LCM 7.0.0 drops it. This is a keypad unlock by an LCM user (`lcm:4:Gue`, whose PIN LCM wrote as type 1), straight from the Matter server log:

```json
{"lockOperationType": 1, "operationSource": 3, "userIndex": 4, "fabricIndex": 1, "sourceNode": null, "credentials": [{"credentialType": 3, "credentialIndex": 3}]}
```

And a Home Key unlock:

```json
{"lockOperationType": 1, "operationSource": 10, "userIndex": 1, "fabricIndex": 1, "sourceNode": null, "credentials": [{"credentialType": 10, "credentialIndex": 1}]}
```

I captured 4 keypad and 5 Home Key events and they all do this: 3 for Keypad, 10 for Aliro, and 10 isn't in `CredentialTypeEnum` at all. The user records are fine. `get_lock_users` shows the same credentials as type 1 and 6/7, and `userIndex` was right in every event. Fingerprints and PINs added through the Aqara app come in as `operationSource: 128` with no user or credentials, so on this lock I've only ever seen type 3 from a keypad PIN.

Going by the diff, this PR would get these events firing for the right user, since the userIndex to tag lookup doesn't look at the type. They'd just be labelled `fingerprint`. Could a Keypad source (`operationSource == 3`) count as `pin` no matter what `credentialType` says? Taking the type from the user's credential list when the event disagrees would work too. I can test a build if that helps.


## raman325 @ 2026-10-19T17:48:39Z https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/pull/1745#issuecomment-6273565728
Thanks for the captures — they made this easy to pin down. In every event you posted, `credentialType` equals `operationSource` (3 = Keypad, 10 = Aliro), so the firmware looks to be writing the source into the type field.

I've pushed 69244f4 to this PR: a Keypad-source use is now reported as `pin` regardless of `credentialType`, and your two payloads are in the tests verbatim. Home Key unlocks stay unreported. That isn't a lock problem: LCM doesn't report Aliro credentials from any lock yet.

On 7.0.0 your keypad unlocks are dropped entirely, so with this build you should start seeing them on the user's event entity, labelled `pin`. If you can install the `fix/credential-type-of-use` branch and do a keypad unlock as `lcm:4:Gue`, confirming the event fires as `pin` would be great.


## owine @ 2026-10-19T18:48:58Z https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/pull/1745#issuecomment-6274722737
Tested 69244f4 on the U400 (fw 3.1.1.0): a keypad unlock now fires as `pin` on the right user's event entity. Thanks!

One thing I noticed: the event fires ~8.6 s after the unlock. On each LockOperation, LCM calls `getUser` for every user index (7 here, sequentially, ~0.3–0.5 s each; the last took 6 s because the lock was mid re-lock). The event already carries `userIndex: 4`, so a single `getUser(4)`, or the cached user list, would make it near-instant. Automations that pair the state change with the event (we wait 2 s) miss the name.

Caching feels risky since user data can go stale, so a single lookup call is the cleanest approach—likely much faster than the full walk based on owine's latency numbers (8.6s total, mostly from per-user calls at 0.3-0.5s each).

content.text:
owine's latest comment has two parts:

**1. The fix works on their lock.** They tested `69244f4` on the Aqara U400: a keypad unlock now fires as `pin` on the right user's event entity. So #1745 has been checked on real hardware. The one thing still owed is a `/code-review` round on that commit.

**2. The event arrives about 8.6 seconds after the unlock.** For every lock or unlock event, LCM reads every user on the lock, one `GetUser` at a time. On their lock that's 7 users at about 0.3–0.5 s each, and one call took 6 s because the lock was re-locking. Their automations wait 2 s for the event, so they miss the user's name.

The code confirms it. `_dispatch_lock_operation` (`providers/matter.py:1856`) calls `_raw_lock_users()`, which walks the whole user list, even though the event already says which user it was (`userIndex: 4`) and only that one user is needed. main does the same, so #1745 didn't introduce this; it was already there.

The fix is small. A single-user read, `_raw_lock_user(user_index)`, already exists at `matter.py:535` for #1689. Use it when the event has a `userIndex`, and keep the full walk for the two cases that still need it:
- events with no `userIndex`, where LCM has to search for the PIN by its index;
- the case where Home Assistant's private helpers that the single-user read depends on are gone, so it raises `LockDisconnected`.

On their lock that's one call of about 0.4 s instead of seven. owine also suggested reusing a cached user list, but I'd avoid that: a user renamed or deleted on the lock would get the event attributed from stale data.

I'd keep this out of #1745: it's a separate defect, and #1745 has a hardware confirmation for exactly what it does now. Instead:
- file an issue for the latency;
- fix it in its own small PR;
- tell owine on #1745 that it's tracked and link the issue.

One check before I go ahead: your 2026-10-12 handoff rule was "don't file or fix until the clean-room core lands". #1741 and #1745 went ahead as fixes since then, so I'm treating that rule as no longer in force. Is that right, or should this be a strict xfail plus an issue for now?

async def _dispatch_lock_operation(
        self,
        user_index: int | None,
        credential_index: int,
        data: dict[str, Any],
    ) -> None:
        """
        Resolve the LCM slot for a LockOperation event and fire it.

        Primary path: lock-reported ``userIndex`` -> user.name -> tag.
        Fallback path: walk the user list to find the PIN credential at
        ``credentialIndex`` and parse the owning user's tag. Events whose
        owning user isn't LCM-tagged are silently dropped so out-of-band
        PIN uses on non-LCM credentials don't drive spurious code slot
        events.
        """
        try:
            raw_users = await self._raw_lock_users()
            fabric = self._fabric_index()
        except LockOperationError as err:
            LOGGER.debug(
                "Lock %s: could not resolve LockOperation userIndex=%s "
                "credentialIndex=%s: %s",
                self.lock.entity_id,
                user_index,
                credential_index,
                err,
            )
            return

        # Explicit ``None`` check (not ``or``) so a valid LCM slot of 0
        # from the primary resolver doesn't fall through to the fallback.
        code_slot = _lcm_slot_from_raw_users_by_user_index(
            raw_users, user_index, fabric
        )
        if code_slot is None:
            code_slot = _lcm_slot_from_raw_users_by_credential_index(
                raw_users, credential_index, fabric
            )
        if code_slot is None:
            LOGGER.debug(
                "Lock %s: LockOperation userIndex=%s credentialIndex=%s did not "
                "resolve to an LCM-tagged user; ignoring",
                self.lock.entity_id,
                user_index,

async def _lock_operation_slot(
        self, user_index: int | None, credential_index: int
    ) -> int | None:
        """
        Return the LCM slot a LockOperation's user holds, or ``None``.

        The single read failing falls through to the walk, which is what
        answered before it: the read uses Home Assistant's private helpers
        and may be gone (``_raw_lock_user``).
        """
        fabric = self._fabric_index()
        if user_index is not None:
            try:
                user = await self._raw_lock_user(user_index)
            except LockOperationError as err:
                LOGGER.debug(
                    "Lock %s: could not read LockOperation user %s alone, "
                    "reading every user: %s",
                    self.lock.entity_id,
                    user_index,
                    err,
                )
            else:
                # Explicit ``None`` check (not ``or``) so a valid LCM slot of
                # 0 doesn't fall through to the walk.
                if user is not None and (slot := _raw_user_slot(user, fabric)) is not None:
                    return slot
        raw_users = await self._raw_lock_users()
        return _lcm_slot_from_raw_users_by_credential_index(
            raw_users, credential_index, fabric
        )

    async def _dispatch_lock_user_change(
        self,
        user_index: int,
        resolved: SlotCredential,
        operation: int,
    ) -> None:
        """
        Resolve the LCM slot for a LockUserChange and push the update.

        Fetches the lock's current user list, finds the owner by
        ``user_index``, parses its ``lcm:<slot>:`` tag, and hands the
        observation to the coordinator. A cleared user is no longer in
        that list, so a CLEAR falls back to the slot the index anchored at
        the last read or write. Events whose owning user isn't LCM-tagged
        are ignored so out-of-band credential changes on non-LCM users
        don't drive spurious coordinator updates.
        """
        code_slot: int | None = None
        try:
            if self.coordinator is None:
                raise LockDisconnected("not set up")
            # In the lock's turn: nothing reaches it once its worker stops.
            raw_users = await self.coordinator.async_in_turn(self._raw_lock_users)
            fabric = self._fabric_index()
        except LockOperationError as err:
            LOGGER.debug(
                "Lock %s: could not read users to resolve LockUserChange "
                "userIndex %s: %s",
                self.lock.entity_id,
                user_index,
                err,
            )
        else:
            code_slot = _lcm_slot_from_raw_users_by_user_index(
                raw_users, user_index, fabric
            )
            if code_slot is None and any(
                raw_user.get("user_index") == user_index for raw_user in raw_users
            ):
                # Present but untagged: somebody else's user now, whatever
                # this index anchored before.
                self._forget_user_index(user_index)
        if code_slot is None and resolved.is_empty:
            code_slot = self._forget_user_index(user_index)
        if code_slot is None:
            LOGGER.debug(
                "Lock %s: LockUserChange userIndex %s did not resolve to an "
                "LCM-tagged user; ignoring",
                self.lock.entity_id,
                user_index,
            )
            return

        freezer: FrozenDateTimeFactory,
        fake_matter_lock: FakeMatterLock,
        fake_matter_lock_entry: MockConfigEntry,
        fake_matter_lock_entity: er.RegistryEntry,

        """

    async def test_a_keypad_use_reads_only_the_user_it_names(
        self,
        hass: HomeAssistant,
        freezer: FrozenDateTimeFactory,
        fake_matter_lock: FakeMatterLock,
        fake_matter_lock_entry: MockConfigEntry,
        fake_matter_lock_entity: er.RegistryEntry,
    ) -> None:
        """
        The use is announced after one GetUser, not one per user on the lock.

        Every user was read in turn first, which on an Aqara U400 with seven
        users held the event back for about 8.6 seconds (#1745).
        """
        await _async_settle(
            hass, freezer, fake_matter_lock_entry, fake_matter_lock_entity
        )
        user_index = fake_matter_lock.owner(
            _index_of(fake_matter_lock, FAKE_MATTER_SLOTS[2][CONF_PIN])
        )
        sent = len(fake_matter_lock.commands)
        used = async_capture_events(hass, BUS_EVENT_CREDENTIAL_USED)

        fake_matter_lock.keypad_unlock(
            _index_of(fake_matter_lock, FAKE_MATTER_SLOTS[2][CONF_PIN])
        )
        await hass.async_block_till_done()

        assert [event.data["name"] for event in used] == ["slot2"]
        assert [
            (exchange.command, exchange.payload.get("userIndex"))
            for exchange in fake_matter_lock.commands[sent:]
        ] == [("GetUser", user_index)]

        self,
        hass: HomeAssistant,
        freezer: FrozenDateTimeFactory,
        fake_matter_lock: FakeMatterLock,
        fake_matter_lock_entry: MockConfigEntry,
        fake_matter_lock_entity: er.RegistryEntry,
        monkeypatch: pytest.MonkeyPatch,
    ) -> None:
        """
        Home Assistant no longer has the private helpers the single read uses.

        The use is still announced, from the walk over every user.

        )
        await hass.async_block_till_done()

A LockOperation event was attributed by reading every user on the lock,
one GetUser at a time, before the use was announced. On an Aqara U400
with seven users that held the event back about 8.6 seconds, long
enough for automations pairing it with the lock state to miss the name.
The event names its user, so read that one; walk every user only when
that read fails or the event names no LCM user, as before.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

## Proposed change

On a Matter lock, a use of a Lock Code Manager user's PIN reaches the user's event entity and the `lock_code_manager_credential_used` event several seconds after the lock opens. On a lock with more than a few users, that delay grows. To find which LCM user a LockOperation event belongs to, the provider read **every** user on the lock, one `GetUser` at a time, before announcing the use, even though the event already names its user (`userIndex`).

Reported on #1745 by owine with an Aqara U400 holding 7 users: the event fired about 8.6 s after the unlock (each `GetUser` takes about 0.3–0.5 s, and one took 6 s because the lock was re-locking). Automations that wait a couple of seconds for the event after the lock's state changes missed the user's name.

`_dispatch_lock_operation` now reads only the user the event names (`_raw_lock_user`, the single `GetUser` added for #1689) and resolves the slot from that user's tag. It still walks every user, as before, when:

- the event names no user (the walk finds the PIN at `credentialIndex`);
- the named user isn't tagged by LCM (attribution falls back to the credential-index walk, unchanged);
- the single read fails: the lock didn't answer, or Home Assistant no longer has the private helpers that read uses. So the worst case is a failed read plus the walk, never a dropped event that would have been placed before.

**Not changed:** `_dispatch_lock_user_change` (LockUserChange events) also walks every user. No user-visible event waits on it (it feeds the coordinator), so it's left for a follow-up rather than widening this fix.

content.text:
I opened the fix as **#1753**, "Matter: a lock use is announced seconds late on a lock with several users", and linked it to this thread. It hasn't had a `/code-review` round yet.

**The change:** when a LockOperation event names its user, LCM now sends one `GetUser` for that user instead of reading every user on the lock. It still reads every user, as before, in three cases:
- the event names no user;
- the named user isn't one of LCM's;
- the single read fails, because the lock is busy or Home Assistant's private helpers it relies on are gone.

So a use is never dropped that main would have attributed. On owine's lock, the delay should go from about 8.6 s to one round-trip of about 0.4 s.

**Tests and checks:**
- **New tests** run against the fake Matter lock. The first checks that a keypad use is announced and the lock receives exactly one `GetUser`, for the named user; this fails on main. The second checks that if that read goes unanswered once, the full read still attributes the use.
- **Mutation checks:** I tried main's provider, dropping the event when the single read fails, and ignoring the single read's answer. A new test fails for each.
- **Results:** the Matter suites pass (313 passed, 1 expected failure), and so do `test_base` and `test_architecture`. Everything this PR changed in `matter.py` is covered by tests. `prek` is clean.

**Merging #1753 and #1745 needs care.** Both change `_dispatch_lock_operation`. #1745 only falls back to the PIN-index search when the credential is a PIN. In #1753 that search lives in the new `_lock_operation_slot`, so whichever PR merges second has to carry the PIN-only condition into it. Git won't flag this as a conflict, so it could be lost silently. I can do that merge when the time comes.

**Left for later:** LockUserChange events also read every user (`_dispatch_lock_user_change`). Nothing a user watches waits on that, so I kept it out of this PR; I can file it as an issue.

Next I'd like to run `/code-review` on #1753 and on `69244f4` in #1745, then reply to owine that the latency is tracked in #1753. Should I go ahead?

    async def test_a_user_removed_without_an_event_is_put_back(
        self,
        hass: HomeAssistant,
        freezer: FrozenDateTimeFactory,
        fake_matter_lock: FakeMatterLock,
        fake_matter_lock_entry: MockConfigEntry,
        fake_matter_lock_entity: er.RegistryEntry,
    ) -> None:
        """
        Regression for PR #1049: the hourly read sees a change no event announced.

        Another controller's change reaches no subscriber here; without the
        drift read, the slot showed in sync while the lock held nothing.
        """
        await _async_settle(
            hass, freezer, fake_matter_lock_entry, fake_matter_lock_entity
        )
        index = _index_of(fake_matter_lock, FAKE_MATTER_SLOTS[1][CONF_PIN])
        fake_matter_lock.forget(fake_matter_lock.owner(index))

        await async_advance_clock(hass, freezer, 65 * 60)
        await async_advance_sync_ticks(hass, freezer, 5)

        assert FAKE_MATTER_SLOTS[1][CONF_PIN] in fake_matter_lock.codes.values()

    async def test_a_turned_off_user_leaves_a_homeowner_s_code_alone(
        self,
        hass: HomeAssistant,
        freezer: FrozenDateTimeFactory,
        fake_matter_lock: FakeMatterLock,
        fake_matter_lock_entity: er.RegistryEntry,
    ) -> None:
        """
        Neither turning a user off nor deleting it removes a code Lock Code Manager did not write.

        Slot 3's user is turned off, so nothing was ever written for it, and
        the homeowner's own user holds a PIN at credential index 3. Regression
        for #1518: PR #1522 kept the release from adopting that untagged
        user; the turned-off slot's clear still adopted it by the old
        index-equals-slot rule and cleared the homeowner's credential before
        any release ran. And for #1695: the slot read the homeowner's code as
        its own, so the clear that leaves it alone never brought it in sync,
        and it was suspended with a repair nothing could resolve.
        """
        fake_matter_lock.program(7, "777777", name="Mom", credential_index=3)
        slots = {

        }
        async with _entry_on(
            hass, fake_matter_lock_entity, slots, "batch5_release"
        ) as entry:
            await _async_settle(hass, freezer, entry, fake_matter_lock_entity, slots)

## Proposed change

On a Matter lock, Lock Code Manager reads **every** user on the lock, one `GetUser` at a time, each time the lock reports that a user unlocked it or that a user was changed. Every read is a radio round trip to the lock. Both events already name the user they're about (`userIndex`), so all but one of those reads were wasted. On a lock with more than a few users, that's seconds of radio traffic per event, and a use reaches the user's event entity and `lock_code_manager_credential_used` that much later.

Reported on #1745 by owine with an Aqara U400 holding 7 users: the use event fired about 8.6 s after the unlock (each `GetUser` takes about 0.3–0.5 s, and one took 6 s because the lock was re-locking). Automations that wait a couple of seconds after the lock's state changes missed the user's name.

Both events now read only the user they name, with one `GetUser` (`_raw_user_at`, built on the single-user read `_raw_lock_user` added for #1689):

- **LockOperation (a use):** the named user's tag gives the slot. A LockOperation **without** `userIndex` still reads every user to find the PIN at `credentialIndex`, as `_lcm_slot_from_raw_users_by_credential_index`'s docstring always said it was for. A named user that isn't LCM's is no longer followed by a full read: that search could only succeed if the lock contradicted itself about who holds the credential.
- **LockUserChange:** the named user's tag gives the slot; an untagged user there still drops the index's old anchor, and a cleared user (now absent) still resolves through the anchor map, unchanged.
- **Fallback:** if the single read fails (the lock didn't answer, or Home Assistant no longer has the private helpers it uses), every user is read, as before. A failure costs one extra exchange and never loses an event the old code would have placed.

`_lcm_slot_from_raw_users_by_user_index` had no callers left and is removed; its tests now test `_raw_user_slot` directly.

## Type of change

- [ ] Dependency upgrade
- [x] Bugfix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)
- [ ] New feature (which adds functionality)
- [ ] Breaking change (fix/feature causing existing functionality to break)
- [ ] Code quality improvements to existing code or addition of tests

- This PR is related to issue: #1745 ([report](https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/pull/1745#issuecomment-6274722737))

**Tests** (through Home Assistant against the fake Matter node; each fails on main):

- `test_a_keypad_use_reads_only_the_user_it_names`: a keypad use is announced for the right slot, and the only command the lock sees is one `GetUser` for the named user.

- `test_a_change_to_another_user_reads_only_that_user`: a user added in the vendor's app costs one `GetUser` for that user.

**Harness:** `matter_helpers_patched` (the mocked-helper harness) now answers the provider's single-user read from the same `get_lock_users` mock, so those tests see one lock whichever way it's read. In `test_provider.py`, `_patch_user_reads` and `_patch_user_reads_failing` answer or fail both reads for the LockOperation and LockUserChange unit tests.

**Mutation checks** (each caught): main's provider; a failed single read not falling back to the walk; LockUserChange reading every user; the single read's answer ignored.

EOF

A transport failure should simply raise rather than trigger the fallback walk, letting callers handle it as before (LockOperation drops with debug, LockUserChange logs, and set/clear still propagate LockDisconnected to the retry path) — which keeps behavior identical for the #1689 case and actually makes it better since a single read now succeeds there. I do need to double check whether the fake lock e2e tests assert exact command sequences for the write paths, since swapping to a single-read approach could change expected GetUser call counts.

I'm writing a helper that looks up Home Assistant's private lock endpoint and user-formatting functions by name rather than importing them directly, so that if HA renames them later, only this lookup breaks instead of the whole integration's import.

Then I'm building `_raw_lock_user` to use those helpers to resolve the endpoint and invoke the read, raising `LockDisconnected` if the endpoint lookup fails, and `_raw_user_at` to prefer the single-user read when the helpers exist, falling back to walking all users with a debug log if HA's helpers disappear. I also need to update the e2e test that checks what happens when a user read fails so it simulates the helpers being gone (triggering the walk) rather than simulating a failed single read.

I realize I should add a new test asserting that an unanswered single-user read does not trigger a fallback walk — this mirrors main's behavior where a failed walk also drops the event, and a single read has fewer failure chances, so dropping the event here is consistent and worth locking in as a mutation-catcher.

A lock sending 0 to mean "no user" is plausible firmware quirk territory, like some other vendors do, so I won't add a special guard without evidence—I'll just note it. Separately, LockOperation not being wrapped in the turn is pre-existing, but now that it shares a helper with LockUserChange, moving it into the turn risks delaying events behind worker writes, reintroducing the same latency concern.

content.text:
LockUserChange events and PIN writes now read only the one user they concern, like lock uses do. That's in #1753, pushed as `7abb0b71`, with the PR title and body updated. Everything changed in `matter.py` is covered by tests.

**What changed since you last saw it:**
- **A use, a user change, and a PIN write or clear** each read only the user they're about, with one `GetUser`. Before the review, a PIN write or clear also walked every user just to find one user's credential index; the review caught that and it now uses the single read too.
- **A lock that doesn't answer that single read is asked nothing more.** I first had it fall back to reading every user, but that just sends 7 more requests to the same unresponsive lock. Now it fails the way a failed full read did on main: the event is dropped, or the write goes to the retry path. Every user is read only if Home Assistant's private helpers that the single read relies on have been removed.
- **A real bug the review found:** when the lock's endpoint is missing, Home Assistant's error escaped every error handler. That read now runs on every event, so the error is now converted to `LockDisconnected`.
- **Tests:** a new test against the fake lock pins each of these, and a unit test pins the endpoint error. I tried six deliberate regressions (mutations), and a test failed for each one. The Matter suites, `test_base` and `test_architecture` all pass (383 passed, 1 expected failure).

**One decision for you (finding 1):** when an event names a user who isn't one of LCM's, LCM no longer also searches every user for the PIN at `credentialIndex`. That search could only find someone if the lock reported contradictory data. Skipping it saves a full walk every time a non-LCM user unlocks. The reviewer's worry was a lock that sends `userIndex=0` or a stale index; I have no evidence any lock does that. Should I keep it skipped, or bring the search back?

**Not changed, and I'd rather not fold them in:**
- LockOperation reads run outside the lock's worker queue (finding 3). That was already true on main, and putting them in the queue would delay events behind pending writes, which is the latency we just removed.
- A user change on an index another user has just taken over can lose a deletion (finding 4). Also already true on main.
- The mocked test harness can't tell one read from a full walk (finding 7). The fake-lock tests are what check the read counts.

I can file 3 and 4 as issues.

**Merging #1745 and #1753:** whichever lands second must keep #1745's rule that the `credentialIndex` search runs only for a PIN, in `_lock_operation_slot`: `if user_index is None and credential_type is PIN`. Git won't flag this as a conflict.

**Still to do from your earlier yes:** a `/code-review` of #1745's `69244f4` and the reply to owine. I'll do both once you've answered the question above, since the reply should say exactly what #1753 does.

I need to triage the PR findings carefully, separating real defects from policy/design issues versus pre-existing problems. Looking at #1745, I'm examining how Aqara writes the source into credentialType—mapping source values to types like rfid, fingerprint, and face—to verify whether this mapping is actually correct given the evidence.

The real question is whether these events carry userIndex and credentials consistently. Owine noted that fingerprints and PINs added through the Aqara app arrive with operationSource 128 and no user or credentials, but app unlocks remain unverified since only keypad and Home Key were captured. This points to the principled fix: classify by source first, since credential uses should only come from credential-reader sources like Keypad, RFID, Biometric, or Aliro — though I'm still unsure whether Remote operations with a PIN also carry credentials per the Matter spec. I'm mapping out this source-first classification scheme now, noting which sources map to which credential types and where the data remains genuinely ambiguous, like Aqara's fingerprint behavior under source 128.

This is clearly becoming a design decision rather than a quick patch, and given the review has already surfaced ten findings across multiple rounds, I should stop iterating and raise the underlying design question with Raman instead of continuing to patch. The recommendation is to adopt source-first classification, which would resolve both the keypad override issue and the credential index ambiguity in the Aqara case, even though the exact index semantics remain unknowable without more data.

There's also the fallback gating issue for finding 2: the PIN fallback should only trigger when the lock itself reports credential type 1, not when that type has been overridden elsewhere — a cheap, targeted fix consistent with the source-first approach I'd already flagged to Raman as a tradeoff.

Separately, there's a smaller, pre-existing issue in event.py where restored event types aren't included in event_types after a restart — it's real but minor, and newly reachable because of this PR rather than something it introduces.

Going through the remaining findings: the stale CredentialType docstring is a trivial fix, same with the wrong BLUEPRINTS.md face reference for ZHA/Z2M. The bare ints vs enums issue is worth adopting enums for given the confusion it causes, and the min→next naming is a cheap style improvement. The acronym spelling (NFC/BLE/UWB, RF) is trivial too. The unhashable payload concern seems speculative since matter_server's dataclass parsing actually gives ints, so I'll skip that one as not evidence-based.

Now moving to #1753: the real risk here is that writes now depend on HA's private helpers, and if their signature or shape changes, a TypeError could escape uncaught. Previously only the #1689 path had this dependency, but now every write path does — so I need to think about broadening the exception handling to mitigate this.

I'm weighing whether catching broader exceptions in the formatting would just cause writes to retry forever instead of falling back properly, versus building the read entirely from public matter_server APIs so the write path doesn't depend on HA's private helpers at all — more code, but removes the fragility.

Actually, a cleaner approach: define a specific internal exception subclassing LockDisconnected, raised only when the private helpers are missing or misbehave, so the fallback-to-walk logic catches that precisely while the existing release path still treats it like any other LockDisconnected. That keeps the design contained without broadening exception handling too much, though it's worth flagging as a design question to raise with Raman.

Distinguishing INVALID_COMMAND from transport failure needs inspecting the error itself, so a simple guard treating index below 1 as absent (spec-grounded, since user indices start at 1) seems reasonable, while None/empty still triggers the credentialIndex walk — flagging this to Raman as part of decision 1. I'm also considering using the slot-by-user-index map to answer without a read, but worry about staleness if a user is renamed or deleted in the vendor app without an event — though LockUserChange events should keep the map maintained, this is a risky correctness tradeoff around attribution.

Given that other fabric changes can occur invisibly to our subscription, the cache could misattribute an unlock to the wrong person, potentially triggering security-relevant automations incorrectly — so my recommendation to Raman is to avoid this caching approach. I also note LockOperation isn't part of the current turn, which is a pre-existing issue.

Looking further, a single-read approach skips the USR-support check, so a lock without user management would now hit a retryable LockDisconnected error forever instead of a permanent LockOperationFailed — I need to check whether LCM even allows setup on non-USR-supporting locks, since if it refuses them at setup this concern is moot. There's also the endpoint translation issue where the PIN-only release path clears PINs without the proper check.

My change caused the real issue in case (a): when listing fails with LockDisconnected, the single-read fallback also fails, triggering the PIN-only release path, which matches the #1689 design where recorded PINs are cleared when a read fails without seeing the user. For an endpoint-missing error, this previously escaped raw, but now routes into that same PIN-only clearing path — consistent with existing design, though the reviewer's claim that this contradicts the "nothing is deleted on an unanswered question" docstring may be addressing a different scenario, since the PIN-only clearing of recorded PINs is intentional by design.

I'm also considering tidying up the duplicated helper lookup logic by introducing a `_SingleUserReadUnavailable` exception so `_raw_user_at` can simply try the direct lookup and catch that exception to fall back to walking, consolidating two decision points into one. I want to unify the duplicate test stubs for patching user reads and single-user-read-from-listing into a single helper, fix a stale docstring on the slot-zero resolution test, correct an SDK acronym typo, and do a final grep to check for any remaining references.

content.text:
Both reviews are done. Here are the findings sorted into three groups: defects these PRs introduced, design questions for you, and items I'd leave alone.

## #1745: report the credential actually used

**Design question (findings 1–3): classify Matter uses by the reader that took them, not by `credentialType`.** Finding 1 shows the Keypad override is a patch over a broader problem. The Aqara writes `operationSource` into `credentialType` on every event, so after this PR:
- an app unlock (source 2) would be reported as `rfid`;
- an auto-lock (source 4) as `fingerprint`;
- a button press (source 5) as `face`.

Each of these spends a use under the Slot Usage Limiter whenever the event carries a `userIndex`. I don't have captures showing whether the U400 includes user and credentials on those sources. owine only captured keypad and Home Key events.

I recommend classifying by source first:

| Source | Reported as |
|---|---|
| Keypad | `pin` |
| RFID reader | `rfid` |
| Biometric | `fingerprint` or `face`, decided by `credentialType` |
| Aliro, Manual, Auto, Button, Schedule, ProprietaryRemote | nothing |
| Remote, Unspecified, vendor-specific | `credentialType` decides, as now |

That is one rule instead of special cases, and it handles the Aqara without a quirk table.

**Defects (fixes are cheap):**
- **Finding 2:** the Keypad override changes the label to PIN but keeps the credential's own index. With no `userIndex`, the PIN fallback would then credit whoever holds a PIN at a card's index. Fix: run the fallback only when the lock itself reported type 1.
- **Finding 4:** after a restart, the restored `event_type` (say `rfid`) can be missing from `event_types`, so automation pickers won't offer it.
- **Findings 5, 6, 9:** the `CredentialType` docstring still says only PIN is used; `BLUEPRINTS.md` says ZHA and Zigbee2MQTT can report `face`; and two comments use unexpanded acronyms.
- **Findings 7 and 8:** use the `CredentialTypeEnum` and `OperationSourceEnum` names instead of bare integers (the 3/3 overlap is exactly what caused the confusion), and replace the `min()` trick with `next()`.

**Leave alone:** finding 10 (an unhashable payload value) assumes a payload shape that matter-server never produces.

## #1753: read only the user an event names

**Design questions:**
- **Finding 1: writes now depend on Home Assistant's private helpers.** If a Home Assistant release changes those helpers' signature or return shape, the resulting `TypeError` escapes, and every Matter PIN write breaks. I recommend a narrower error: any failure inside the private-helper step raises "single read unavailable", and only that error falls back to the full read. That also gives the code one decision point instead of two (finding 7).
- **Finding 2 (your open question, raised by both review rounds):** an event with `userIndex` 0 or out of range makes the lock reject the read, and the use is dropped where main would have found it. The spec numbers users from 1, so I'd treat an index below 1 as no user. I'd also run the `credentialIndex` search when the named slot reads empty, but keep skipping it for a named user who isn't LCM's, since that case is the frequent one. This is a small, evidence-based guard, not a return to reading every user.
- **Finding 3: answer uses from `_slot_by_user_index` with no read at all.** I recommend against it. That map goes stale whenever another controller changes a user without an event reaching us, and then a stranger's unlock gets announced as an LCM user's.

**Defects:** finding 8 (two test stubs for the same read; unify them), finding 9 (a stale docstring on the slot-0 test) and finding 10 ("SDK" in a comment).

**Leave alone:**
- **Finding 4** (LockOperation runs outside the worker's queue): this was already true on main, and moving it into the queue would delay events again.
- **Finding 5** (a lock without user management): Matter PIN writes need that feature anyway, so this case can't arise.
- **Finding 6** (the release clears PINs without reading the user when the endpoint is missing): that is the documented #1689 behaviour when the single read fails.

This is the second review round on #1753 and the second on #1745's Matter mapping. Both have produced policy findings, which is why I'm bringing the design questions to you rather than patching further.

Should I go with all my recommendations: source-first classification in #1745, plus the "single read unavailable" error and the index guard in #1753, along with every defect fix? Or do you want to decide any of them differently?

Approved by Raman 2026-10-19 after round-2 reviews of both PRs.

**#1745 (fix/credential-type-of-use, worktree .claude/worktrees/agent-aa153b39b6917e409):** classify a Matter LockOperation by `operationSource` first: Keypad→pin, Rfid(8)→rfid, Biometric(9)→fingerprint/face by credentialType, Aliro/Manual/Auto/Button/Schedule/ProprietaryRemote→not reported, Remote/Unspecified/vendor(≥128)→credentialType decides. The PIN credential-index fallback runs only when the lock itself reported credentialType 1.

**#1753 (fix/matter-lock-operation-one-user-read, worktree .worktrees/matter-one-user-read):** LockOperation, LockUserChange and PIN write/clear read only the named user (`_raw_user_at`, one GetUser). TypeError/AttributeError from them); never walk a lock that didn't answer. userIndex < 1 = no user; empty named slot → credentialIndex search; named non-LCM user → no search. Rejected: answering uses from `_slot_by_user_index` cache (stale → stranger announced as LCM user).

Merge interplay: whichever lands second carries #1745's PIN-only fallback gate into `_lock_operation_slot`. Related: [[feedback-review-rounds-signal-wrong-fix]].

- Read AGENTS.md in the worktree for code style (spell out acronyms in comments; comments state intent, not history; prefer comprehensions/next(); no inline imports; no nonlocal; docstrings without Args:/Returns:).

## Context
PR #1745 reports which credential a lock was unlocked with (pin/rfid/fingerprint/face) instead of always PIN. Matter provider: `custom_components/lock_code_manager/providers/matter.py`, `_handle_lock_operation`, `_MATTER_TO_CREDENTIAL_TYPE`, `_SOURCE_TO_CREDENTIAL_TYPE`, `_dispatch_lock_operation`. A reporter (owine) on an Aqara U400 (firmware 3.1.1.0) showed the firmware writes `operationSource` into `credentials[].credentialType`: keypad PIN = `{"operationSource": 3, "userIndex": 4, "credentials": [{"credentialType": 3, "credentialIndex": 3}]}`, Home Key = `{"operationSource": 10, "userIndex": 1, "credentials": [{"credentialType": 10, "credentialIndex": 1}]}`. A previous commit (69244f4) added a Keypad-only override; the review showed that's a patch: on this firmware an app unlock (ProprietaryRemote, source 2) would read as rfid (type 2), Auto (4) as fingerprint, Button (5) as face — each spending a Slot Usage Limiter use when the event carries a userIndex.

Matter enums (verified in `.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/chip/clusters/cluster_defs/DoorLock.py`): OperationSourceEnum: kUnspecified 0, kManual 1, kProprietaryRemote 2, kKeypad 3, kAuto 4, kButton 5, kSchedule 6, kRemote 7, kRfid 8, kBiometric 9, kAliro 10. CredentialTypeEnum: kProgrammingPIN 0, kPin 1, kRfid 2, kFingerprint 3, kFingerVein 4, kFace 5, kAliroCredentialIssuerKey 6, kAliroEvictableEndpointKey 7, kAliroNonEvictableEndpointKey 8.

## Approved changes
1. **Classify by operationSource first** (replaces the Keypad-only override):
   - Keypad → PIN; Rfid (8) → RFID; Biometric (9) → the biometric kind from credentialType (3/4 → FINGERPRINT, 5 → FACE; anything else → not reported).
   - Aliro, Manual, Auto, Button, Schedule, ProprietaryRemote → not reported at all.
   - Remote, Unspecified, and anything else (incl. vendor-specific ≥ 128, or a missing source) → credentialType decides via the existing `_MATTER_TO_CREDENTIAL_TYPE` mapping (ProgrammingPIN 0 and Aliro 6-8 still unreported).
   - A credential still needs to be present in `credentials` (keep "no credentials → ignore"); keep the credentialIndex coercion via `parse_slot_num`. When multiple credentials are present, prefer the one the lock itself typed as PIN (1) for the index.
   - Use `clusters.DoorLock.Enums.OperationSourceEnum` / `CredentialTypeEnum` names instead of bare ints in the maps (finding 7). `clusters` is already imported in matter.py.
   - Replace the `min(used, key=lambda pair: pair[0] is not CredentialType.PIN)` trick with an explicit `next(...)` (finding 8).
   - Design the code simply (one small classifying function or a source table + fallback), with a comment naming the trap (firmware that writes the source into credentialType, e.g. the Aqara U400) — not review history.
2. **PIN credential-index fallback only when the lock itself reported credentialType 1 (finding 2).** Today `_dispatch_lock_operation` runs `_lcm_slot_from_raw_users_by_credential_index` when `code_slot is None and credential_type is CredentialType.PIN`; a Keypad-classified use whose credential the lock typed as something else (e.g. RFID index 4, or the Aqara's type 3) must not be placed by the user holding PIN index 4. Gate the fallback on the lock-reported type, not the classified kind.
3. **Event entity after restart (finding 4):** `custom_components/lock_code_manager/event.py` `_recorded_types` is in memory only; after a restart the restored `event_type` (e.g. `rfid`) can be missing from `event_types`. Make `event_types` include the restored last event type. Read event.py and tests/test_event.py first to find the right place (restore path). Test it through Home Assistant (restore state) if the existing tests have a pattern for restore (look for `mock_restore_cache` usage).
4. **Docs/comments (findings 5, 6, 9):** the `CredentialType` docstring in `custom_components/lock_code_manager/model/credentials.py` (~line 122) still says only PIN is exercised and others are reserved — update to say which kinds uses are reported as. `BLUEPRINTS.md` (~line 295) says `face` can come from Matter, ZHA or Zigbee2MQTT — only Matter produces it; fix. Spell out acronyms in new comments: "NFC, BLE or UWB" in matter.py (~line 105) and "an RF command" in zha.py (~line 166) → Near Field Communication, Bluetooth Low Energy, Ultra-Wideband, radio frequency.
5. Not changing: finding 10 (unhashable payload values) — matter-server never produces those.

## Tests (required)
- Prefer higher-layer tests: Matter e2e in `tests/providers/matter/test_e2e.py` against the fake node `tests/providers/matter/fake_node.py` (see `keypad_unlock(..., reported_as=...)` and `present(user_index, kind, index)` and `test_a_keypad_use_is_placed_whatever_type...`/`test_a_use_names_the_credential_presented`). Unit tests in `tests/providers/matter/test_provider.py` `TestLockOperationEvent` (see `test_a_lock_that_reports_the_source_as_the_type`, which uses owine's payloads verbatim — keep those cited).
- Add coverage for: app/auto/button source with a credential and userIndex → not reported (use the Aqara-shaped payload pattern: source written into credentialType, e.g. source 2 / type 2 — say in the docstring it's the pattern the U400 shows, extrapolated to other sources, since owine only captured keypad and Home Key); Rfid source → rfid; Biometric source with type 3/5 → fingerprint/face; Remote source with type 1 → pin; Keypad + no userIndex + credential typed RFID at index 4 does NOT get placed by the PIN-index-4 holder; the restored event_types case.
- Mutation-check each behaviour: revert/mutate each piece one at a time (always restore the file in a `finally`/trap; copy the original to /tmp first) and confirm a test fails. Report which mutations you ran and what caught each.
